one_liner: Drop-in Go regexp replacement using 17 pattern-specific engines and SIMD prefilters; beats Rust regex on literal-heavy patterns only.
what_it_does: coregex replaces Go stdlib's single generic NFA regexp engine with a compiler that extracts literals from the pattern and dispatches to one of 17 specialized search strategies (LazyDFA, PikeVM, OnePass, BoundedBacktracker, Teddy, Aho-Corasick, reverse-suffix/inner DFAs, etc.). It implements 100% of the stdlib regexp API (per docs/STDLIB_COMPATIBILITY.md), so most call sites need no code change beyond the import path. Backreferences are unsupported by design, preserving stdlib's O(n)/no-ReDoS guarantee.
how_it_is_fast: At compile time it extracts required literals (prefix, suffix, inner substring, digit runs) and routes to an engine built for that shape instead of one generic NFA: SIMD memchr/memmem (AVX2/SSSE3) for single-literal search, Slim/Fat Teddy or Aho-Corasick for multi-literal alternation, and reverse (right-to-left) DFA search for suffix/inner-literal patterns that skips most of the input entirely. Patterns without a strong literal anchor fall back to LazyDFA, PikeVM, OnePass, or BoundedBacktracker.
when_to_use: Pattern has an extractable literal (suffix like .*\.log, inner substring like .*error.*, an IP/digit run, or an anchored prefix): reverse-DFA/prefilter paths ran 1.2x-52x faster than Rust regex on kolkov/regex-bench.
Migrating a Go codebase off stdlib regexp for CPU-bound matching where the 100%-API-compatible surface (per docs/STDLIB_COMPATIBILITY.md) avoids a rewrite.
Deploying on amd64 with AVX2/SSSE3 available (the benchmark ran on a GitHub Actions AMD EPYC runner); SIMD prefilters only exist on that architecture.
A zero-allocation hot loop over many matches: AllIndex/AppendAllIndex iterators are up to 30% faster than FindAll per the README.
Multi-pattern literal alternation (foo|bar|baz, roughly 2-64 literals) handled by the Teddy or Aho-Corasick engines.
when_not_to_use: Pattern is alternation-heavy without a literal anchor, has bounded-repeat groups, or is a plain character class: coregex was 1.8x-7.4x slower than Rust regex on 8 of 16 kolkov/regex-bench patterns (email, uri, literal_alt, http_methods, multi_literal, alpha_digit, word_digit, word_repeat).
Backreferences are required: not supported (by design, to keep the O(n) guarantee) — use regexp2 instead.
Target is not amd64: SIMD paths are disabled and it falls back to pure Go, so the Rust-beating numbers do not apply there.

Toolchain is older than what the module requires: go.mod pins `go 1.27.1`, while the README's stated minimum ("Go 1.25+") is lower and inconsistent with go.mod — verify against your own Go version before adopting.

Correctness-sensitive code relying on stdlib's exact empty-match positions or repeated-capture-group semantics: docs/STDLIB_COMPATIBILITY.md lists these as unresolved known differences, and the tracker shows a steady stream of matching bugs (dot-vs-codepoint, anchors, negated classes, case-insensitivity) fixed between Dec 2025 and Mar 2026.

integration.min_toolchain: go.mod declares `go 1.27.1`; README separately claims "Go 1.25+" — the two disagree, go.mod is the binding constraint for `go build`
integration.platforms: amd64 with AVX2/SSSE3 for SIMD prefilters; other architectures use a pure-Go fallback (per the record's tradeoffs field, not independently verified this session on non-amd64)
integration.thread_safety: compiled *Regexp is safe for concurrent use by multiple goroutines, using an internal sync.Pool for per-search state (per README)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — 100% of the stdlib regexp API is implemented (docs/STDLIB_COMPATIBILITY.md), but documented behavioral differences remain in empty-match counts/positions, repeated capture-group results, and some combined-flag case-insensitive edge cases

gotchas: Repeated capture groups like (a)* can capture a different iteration than stdlib's "last match" behavior (docs/STDLIB_COMPATIBILITY.md).
Empty-match count and position can differ from stdlib on patterns such as [a-c]*, .*, ^ — documented as an open, unresolved difference.
No backreference support at all; RE2-syntax only.

Two open performance issues on the tracker at verification time: #153 (FindAllStringIndex slower than stdlib in some cases) and #120 (Teddy SIMD 8.6x slower than Rust due to Go/assembly call-boundary overhead).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: It's the only catalogued regex engine targeting Go; the other siblings (nim-regex, rejit, SafeRE, BLARE, RE#, nanoregex, re2jit) are for Nim, C++/RE2, Java, .NET, and Python. Pick coregex specifically when you're on Go stdlib regexp and your patterns are literal-anchored (suffix/inner/prefix); the siblings aren't options in a Go codebase.
verified_claims_summary: On kolkov/regex-bench's cross-language corpus (6.0 MB generated text, 16 real-world patterns, FindAll, coregex v0.12.23, Rust regex 1.11 built with --release/LTO/codegen-units=1, Go 1.23, on a GitHub Actions AMD EPYC runner), coregex beat Rust regex on 6 of 16 patterns (1.2x-52x: version, char_class, multiline_php, suffix, ip, inner_literal), lost on 8 of 16 (1.8x-7.4x slower: uri, alpha_digit, word_digit, http_methods, multi_literal, email, word_repeat, literal_alt), and tied on 2 anchored patterns. Against Go stdlib regexp it was 3.6x-893x faster on all 16 patterns.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-06), MIT-licensed, 261 stars; the issue tracker shows a fast-closing but frequent stream of correctness bugs fixed between Dec 2025 and Mar 2026, indicating a young engine rather than one battle-hardened over years like Rust regex.
